name: QOA (Quite OK Audio)
workload: Encode and decode speed of a simple time-domain lossy audio format versus Opus and MP3 on music files, as reported in the author's launch post and Hacker News discussion.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: 'QOA encodes 10x faster and decodes 7x faster than Opus'; '25.75 seconds to encode a 9807-second file, 5.7 times faster than MP3 encoding on an i7-6700k'; decoding faster than Opus on an i7-6700k single-threaded. The repo itself states only 'fast, lossy audio compression' with no numbers.
stars_or_usage: 985 stars; supported in Godot 4.3, raylib, SerenityOS, Qmmp, OpenCubicPlayer
tradeoffs: Fixed-rate lossy time-domain codec (LMS predictor plus quantisation), far simpler than Opus. HN comment snippets say Opus is better in every way except complexity and CPU cost, and that QOA compresses less than MP3 and sounds worse. Best fit is games or microcontrollers that need cheap decoding. Single-header C/C++ API. Format has a 31 channel limit (latest commit message).
caveats: Numbers come only from Hacker News result snippets (the thread and the author's blog post were not opened; phoboslab.org, qoaformat.org and news.ycombinator.com are blocked here). The repo README and qoa.h contain no benchmark, so the verifier needs the blog post or a rerun. Compiler, flags and files are unknown. The README warns the implementation has not been fuzzed and must not be used with untrusted input. Ported implementations (qoa-fu, qoaudio, goqoa and others) are wrappers or ports of the same format.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN audio codec faster than Opus libopus' then 'Show HN QOA Quite OK Audio format fast lossy audio compression'; threads 'The Quite OK Audio Format for Fast, Lossy Compression' (item 37047343), 'QOA, the Quite OK Audio Format' (item 34625573), 'Quite OK Audio Format' (item 35738817)

name: rav1e
workload: AV1 video encoding speed; the README positions rav1e for cases where libaom is too slow, with speed presets 0-10.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'The fastest and safest AV1 encoder.' and 'in its current form it is most suitable for cases where libaom (the reference encoder) is too slow.'
tradeoffs: Written in Rust with hand-written x86_64 NASM and NEON assembly; needs NASM 2.14.02 or newer and Rust 1.85 or newer. A C API can be built (README section 'Building the C-API'), so it is callable from C++. 11 speed settings from exhaustive to near real-time.
caveats: The README gives no benchmark. The HN thread snippet 'The fastest and safest AV1 encoder but it's also 62.1% assembly?' questions the claim, and other AV1 encoders such as SVT-AV1 are commonly reported as faster; I did not verify that here. Report as tier D only because the project is notable. A verifier should find a public benchmark (for example Phoronix or AOM Codec Working Group tests) or retier it.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN AV1 encoder in 66 KB of safe Rust WASM' surfaced threads 'Rav1e, an AV1 encoder written in Rust and assembly' (item 23512161) and 'Rav1e: An experimental AV1 video encoder, designed to be fast and safe' (item 17539361)

name: xin26x
workload: Single-thread low-delay (IPPP, no B-frames) HEVC encoding at 1080p and 720p on four YUV sequences at fixed bitrates, comparing encode FPS and PSNR with x265.
claimed_speedup: README: 'The performance of xin26x(HEVC) is x4 compared to x265 under single unit core.' Table rows (xin26x FPS vs x265 FPS, PSNR in dB): BasketballDrive 1080p 20.68 vs 7.96 (36.929 vs 36.913); pedestrian_area 1080p 39.203 vs 8.35 (39.719 vs 39.707); KristenAndSara 720p 103.68 vs 23.56 (43.218 vs 43.183); sc_desktop 1080p 39.48 vs 16.83 (40.082 vs 29.817). Ratios 2.60x, 4.69x, 4.40x, 2.35x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Compiler and flags for both binaries are not stated (builds via CMake and Visual Studio 2022 on Windows). Commands: xin26x_test.exe -a 0 -I 0 --wpp 0 --thread 1 --preset 0 (preset 3 for BasketballDrive) --bframes 0; x265.exe --preset fast -I -1 --pools 1 --bframes 0 --frame-threads 0 --no-wpp --tune psnr. README says x265 is the 2020/12/25 version (stated for the offline table).
tradeoffs: Encoder framework for HEVC and VVC (AV1 is intra-frame only and unoptimised pure C). Plain C API (xin_app_enc.c shows usage). Needs x86 with AVX2; max resolution 3860x2160; max 3 temporal layers; AGPL-3.0 copyleft. Optimised for real-time communication, so it lacks some offline tools (the README says lookahead and cu-tree were enabled for fairness in the offline comparison).
caveats: First-party table only; CPU model is not stated and the test sequences are not in the repo (only a Google Drive link to output bitstreams). xin26x presets differ per sequence (preset 3 for one, preset 0 for the rest), so the settings are not matched to x265 fast beyond similar PSNR. x265 build is from 2020-12-25, long out of date. The sc_desktop row is not like for like (xin26x used a screen-content tool, PSNR 40.082 versus 29.817 for x265). README also shows a BD-rate table against x265 veryslow that was not examined for speed. Repo history starts 2026-04 per the commits page.
found_via: Not an HN thread. Hacker News pass was thin; found on github.com/topics/video-codec (sorted by stars) while following up HN leads, then opened the README

name: fcvvdp
workload: Computing the CVVDP perceptual video quality metric between a reference and an x264-encoded 360p video (302 frames), measured with the poop benchmark tool, 3 runs each.
claimed_speedup: README: 'fcvvdp uses over 91% less memory. With one thread, it is over 28% faster; with multiple threads, fcvvdp is over 221% faster than the reference implementation.' Wall time 19.1 s (cvvdp) vs 14.9 s (fcvvdp -t 1, -21.7%) vs 5.94 s (fcvvdp -t 8, -68.9%); peak RSS 1.03 GB vs 90.4 MB vs 89.7 MB.
tradeoffs: Library (libcvvdp with cvvdp.h) plus CLI and an FFmpeg filter patch, so usable from C++. It is a quality metric, not a codec, so it only replaces the reference CVVDP scorer. AVX2 and NEON kernels plus a portable C path; build needs the Zig toolchain (src has C files plus main.zig). Supports sRGB PNG, PNM/PAM, QOI and Y4M input.
caveats: First-party single-clip benchmark; the input clip (fm360p.y4m) is not shipped and the reference's PyTorch device and version are not stated. The README does not state how closely scores match the reference implementation. 8-thread run executes 21.6% more instructions than the reference. The README's percentage wording (28% and 221% faster) is derived from wall-time ratios 19.1/14.9 and 19.1/5.94. Language is C core with Zig build and CLI; GitHub's primary-language label was not visible.
